item.title: “Cosmic Origins” Family Event — Sat Oct 24, 11:00 AM — Center for Documentary Studies

item.title: Shia Islamic-Jewish Legal Reasoning in Dialogue — Sun Oct 25, 8:00 AM — Langford 152
item.description:
Over the last four years, the Shia Islamic-Jewish Legal Reasoning in Dialogue has brought together 13 scholars from across the U.S. and internationally to study legal texts of both traditions via diverse methodologies of academic analysis. They have been divided into 6 working groups working on the topics of the legal self, constitutionalism, theocracy, language, female clerical authority, and the persecution of heretics. The Dialogue is not merely meant to identify similarities and differences, but to allow scholars to think their "own" tradition conceptually anew through this encounter. The project arrives at Duke in order to present its findings and receive constructive critique from Triangle-area scholars of co-written book chapters that will eventually be published in Rutgers University Press' "Transmodern Times" series.
More information at: https://jewishstudies.duke.edu/shia-islamic-jewish-legal-reasoning-dialogue

item.title: ADULT FORUM - "The Gown Speaks First: What the Church Hears BEFORE a Sermon Begins" — Sun Oct 25, 9:45 AM — Westbrook 0012
item.description:
Before a preacher reaches the sermon's first sentence, a congregation is already learning whom to trust. A Geneva gown. A rhinestoned stole. A preacher's voice breaking into song. Each can teach a room what authority is supposed to look and sound like-and who seems strangely out of place. Drawing on his recently published article in the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, Brett McKinley Pardue brings Christian vesture into conversation with drag performance and the visual and sonic life of worship. What does preaching communicate before words-and what if faithful authority arrives dressed differently than we expect?
The Congregation's weekly Adult Forum offers a variety of guest speakers, presentations and discussions on a wide range of thought-provoking topics, including Biblical studies, current social issues and the work of mission agencies. item.title: CEE Seminar - Understanding and Computation of Deformation and Failure in Porous Microstructures — Mon Oct 26, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: This talk presents a body of work aimed at closing that gap, premised on the idea that a sharper physical understanding of how porous solids fail is what enables good approximations of it. Mechanical stress in a loaded microstructure concentrates at the geometric constrictions of the solid, which we hypothesize to be the preferred sites for cracks to nucleate under most loads. This is the basis for a reduced-order model that foreshadows where cracks form and thereby gains several orders of magnitude in computational speed. This hypothesis, which was first supported by phase-field simulations, is now being confirmed by in-situ tensile experiments on 3D-printed porous specimens. Underlying these approximations is a pore-level multiscale method (PLMM) that decomposes the solid into subdomains with local, physics-based closures. item.title: CDVS Workshop: Sharing Human Participants Data: Challenges and (Potential) Solutions — Tue Oct 27, 10:00 AM — Online
item.description:
The sharing of research data has become increasingly important to federal and private funders and journal publishers for a number of reasons (research transparency, reproducibility, return on investment, new research on existing data, etc.). With the latest requirements from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for Data Management and Sharing Plans (https://sharing.nih.gov/), there are legitimate concerns about how data from human beings can ethically and safely be shared. This workshop will talk about the various challenges that arise when considering how to share human participants data in DMSPs and potential ways that these challenges can be addressed, and even solved, with resources available at Duke and beyond (data sharing consent language, controlled access repositories, de-identification help, etc.). This event is open to non-Duke participants. This workshop is eligible for 2 hours of Graduate School RCR Credit (GS714) and 200-level faculty and staff RCR.

item.title: Astronomy & Astrophysics Research Day — Sat Nov 7, 10:00 AM — Downtown Raleigh
item.description: The NC Museum of Natural Sciences is a research-based museum with Museum staff who conduct novel research and steward our collections. Our Research Highlight Days feature these researchers and their fields of study. This event will be held on the first and third floors of the Nature Research Center. Join us as we celebrate Astronomy and Astrophysics Research at this event! Exhibits and Activities Spiral Graph: Cluster Buster We will demonstrate and discuss Spiral Graph: Cluster Buster, our online citizen science project dedicated to identifying individual arms in spiral galaxies and measuring their winding. The degree of winding serves as a proxy for properties such as the mass of the dark matter halo and the mass of the black hole found in a galaxy’s nucleus. Our goal is to find galaxies that will help us understand the co-formation and co-evolution of spiral galaxies and their central supermassive black holes. item.description:
Have you ever noticed how much hotter a parking lot feels than a tree-lined street on a summer day? Even within the same city, temperatures can vary dramatically over surprisingly short distances. But what causes these differences, and what can we do to make our cities cooler? Cities are often hotter than their rural surroundings, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. As climate change brings rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves, understanding how heat varies within cities is becoming increasingly important.
In this talk, Dr. Berk will lead us to explore multitudes of factors that influence urban temperatures, using her findings from right here in Durham and Raleigh. She will also share what we can do about urban heat: from planting trees to installing reflective pavements, which strategies actually work, and how can science help us create cooler, healthier cities.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Thu Jan 21 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.
